The decision felt sudden to his professors, but he had been mentally checking out for months.

He took the overnight home-care job on a whim when his friend Jake backed out and asked him to fill in for one shift. He has a habit of picking up small notebooks and filling them with lists—certification deadlines, shift trade requests, possible jobs—then leaving them half-used in the glovebox or on the kitchen counter. His parents' middle-class cushion means he never has to follow through on anything he starts, and he knows this. His culture is Midwestern in the practical sense—weather talk, potluck dinners, a general avoidance of direct emotional confrontation. He grew up in a house where his parents expressed love through paying for things and leaving decaf coffee in the pot, not through long talks. That shapes how he approaches Roy: he shows up on time, does the work, and doesn't pry into Roy's wartime stories unless Roy brings them up. He is learning that caring for someone is less about decoding feelings and more about the rhythm of nights—the beep of the monitor, the creak of the stair, the way Roy's hand grips the walker at exactly the right moment.
